domain: Disaster Anthropology / Commitment System Analysis / Institutional Memory
topic_summary: Analysis of the Aneyoshi tsunami stone's 'do not build below this line' inscription as a commitment system tested across 78 years of non-catastrophe, culminating in the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The kernel contest is whether the commitment decayed to commemorative symbol or retained live behavioral force. The 2011 event provides a D5 catastrophe-theorem break: the village's survival (building compliance) vs neighboring villages' destruction (compliance failure) offers decisive temporal evidence on commitment vitality.

key_entities: Tsunami stone marker (1933 inscription: 'high dwellings ensure peace and happiness to our descendants')
Neighboring coastal villages (destroyed in 2011; non-compliant settlement patterns)
1933 Showa-Sanriku tsunami (precipitating catastrophe; 3000+ deaths; stone placement event)
2011 Tōhoku tsunami (testing catastrophe; 18,500+ deaths; stone validation event)
key_tensions: Commemorative decay vs behavioral persistence (78-year gap between catastrophes)
Individual economic incentive (coastal access, flat land value) vs collective survival commitment
key_claims: Aneyoshi maintained stone-line compliance through 2011 (empirical: village survived with zero tsunami deaths)
Neighboring villages violated equivalent elevation constraints (empirical: catastrophic losses in 2011)
78-year inter-catastrophe gap tests commitment durability under non-reinforcement
Stone inscription retained behavioral force rather than decaying to symbol

axiom_contradictions.basis: Commemorative decay assumes inscription lost behavioral force and compliance was coincidental; behavioral competence assumes inscription retained causal efficacy. No coherent framework holds both: either the norm was causally operative (and compliance was functional) or it was not (and survival was fortuitous). The 2011 binary outcome adjudicates between them.
